title: The unseen reality of heaven
theme: The unseen reality of heaven, Christ as the meeting place between heaven and earth, and the promise that what we now know through faith will one day be fully revealed
prayer: Prayer  Lord, when what I see makes it difficult to understand what You are doing, remind me that my sight is limited but Your Kingdom is not. Thank You for the angels who serve You and for Michael, Gabriel and Raphael, whose presence reminds us of the reality beyond what our eyes can see. Keep me without duplicity before You, knowing there is nothing in me You have not already seen. Help me trust the victory of Christ even when the world around me does not look victorious. Until the day all things are fully revealed, keep my eyes fixed on Jesus, where heaven and earth meet. Amen.
body:
I think this one should retain the sense of discovery you had while moving among the three readings. The archangels matter, Nathanael matters, Jacob’s ladder matters, and the Parousia matters—but they should gradually reveal one central thought rather than become separate explanations: what we see is not all that is happening.

There Is More Than What We See

Scripture: Daniel 7:9–10, 13–14 or Revelation 12:7–12ab; Psalm 138; John 1:47–51

Theme: The unseen reality of heaven, Christ as the meeting place between heaven and earth, and the promise that what we now know through faith will one day be fully revealed

Opening: What if the world we can see is only part of what is actually happening?

Reflection

Today’s readings left me thinking about something I rarely stop to consider: how much of reality I cannot see.

In the Gospel, Jesus sees Nathanael coming toward Him and says, “Here is a true child of Israel. There is no duplicity in him.” That word, duplicity, stayed with me, especially after reflecting recently on hypocrisy. Nathanael is not perfect. He had just questioned whether anything good could come from Nazareth. But he is not pretending. There is no hidden version of himself being presented as something else.

Nathanael seems almost startled by Jesus’ words. “How do you know me?”

Jesus tells him that He saw him under the fig tree before Philip called him. We aren’t told exactly what happened there, but whatever those words meant to Nathanael, they were enough. He responds, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel.”

Then Jesus essentially tells him: You believe because of this? You are going to see greater things.

“You will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”

That image took me back to Jacob’s ladder, when Jacob dreams of a stairway between earth and heaven with angels ascending and descending upon it. But now there is no ladder.

There is Jesus.

Christ Himself is where heaven and earth meet.

And suddenly today’s readings about the archangels began to look different to me. Daniel is given a glimpse beyond what human eyes ordinarily see: the Ancient One upon His throne, thousands upon thousands ministering before Him, and one like a Son of Man receiving an everlasting dominion.

Revelation pulls the curtain back even further. Michael and his angels are fighting the dragon. Satan, the accuser, is defeated and cast down. There is a battle occurring within a reality that we cannot see with our eyes, yet we experience its consequences.

I found myself wondering why Revelation says Satan was cast down to earth. Why earth? But maybe I was thinking too physically, as though Revelation were describing coordinates in the universe. Earth is where we are. It is where humanity lives out this struggle, where Christ entered human history, and where we experience a victory that has already been won while still living among suffering, temptation, evil and death.

That is difficult to comprehend.

Christ has already conquered sin and death, yet sin and death remain around us. Michael has defeated the dragon, yet the battle certainly seems to continue. Heaven and earth have been joined in Christ, yet heaven remains largely hidden from our sight.

We are living between what has already happened and what has not yet been fully revealed.

And then there is the Parousia—the return of Christ in glory.

I have heard that word before, but today’s readings made me think differently about it. Maybe the Second Coming is not simply Jesus arriving sometime in the future. It is also the fulfillment and revelation of something that is already true: Christ is King. His victory is real. Heaven is real. The Kingdom is real. What we cannot presently see is not therefore absent.

That brings me back to Nathanael.

He is standing before an ordinary-looking man from Nazareth. Only moments earlier, he had questioned whether anything good could even come from there. Yet standing before him is the One upon whom angels ascend and descend, the very meeting place of heaven and earth.

Nathanael could see Jesus.

He could not yet see everything that Jesus was revealing.

Maybe neither can we.

We see what is immediately in front of us. We see suffering, war, sickness, injustice, temptation and death. We also see love, beauty, mercy and goodness. But we cannot see the whole reality in which any of it exists.

That can be frightening, but strangely it also gives me hope.

Because sometimes what I can see doesn’t look victorious at all.

Sometimes evil seems incredibly powerful. Sometimes suffering makes God seem very far away. Sometimes the visible circumstances of our lives give us little reason to believe anything greater is happening.

And yet today’s readings tell us not to confuse what is visible with everything that is real.

Daniel saw beyond it.

John saw beyond it.

Nathanael was told that he would see beyond it.

And the angels remind us that God’s creation extends far beyond what our senses can perceive.

Maybe faith asks us to live within that mystery without pretending we can see through it. We don’t know everything occurring beyond our sight. We don’t understand how every struggle fits within God’s work. But we know the One standing between heaven and earth.

Jesus.

And maybe Nathanael’s question is more important than I first realized: “How do you know me?”

Before Nathanael understood Jesus, Jesus already knew Nathanael.

Before Nathanael could see what was happening in heaven, heaven had already seen him.

There is something deeply comforting in that.

I do not have to see everything to be seen by God.

One day, what is hidden will be revealed. Until then, I live here, somewhere between what Christ has already accomplished and what I am still waiting to see.

And when the world in front of me makes me wonder where God is, I want to remember today’s readings.

There is more happening than what I can see.
